items.body:
### Summary

`BoundRow._get_and_render_with` special-cases any column accessor that resolves to a model field with `choices` and calls the model's `get_FOO_display()` to produce the cell value ([rows.py#L142-L156](https://github.com/jieter/django-tables2/blob/e52d5bc/django_tables2/rows.py#L142-L156)):

```python
# If the penultimate is a model and the remainder is a field
# using choices, use get_FOO_display().
if isinstance(penultimate, models.Model):
    try:
        field = accessor.get_field(self.record)
        display_fn = getattr(penultimate, f"get_{remainder}_display", None)
        if getattr(field, "choices", ()) and display_fn:
            value = display_fn()
            remainder = None
    except FieldDoesNotExist:
        pass
```

This runs once per cell, before the column's own `render()`/`value()`. With classic tuple choices that is a cheap dict build per cell. But since Django 5.0, `choices` **may be a callable**, and Django re-evaluates it on every `field.flatchoices` access — which `_get_FIELD_display()` performs on each call. When the callable loads choices from the database (e.g. codes from a reference table, [as suggested in the Django docs](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/models/fields/#field-choices)), the result is **one query per cell**.

We hit this in production: a 750-row table with two such columns issued ~1,500 identical full-table queries and took ~30 seconds to render. Profiling was confusing because the column's own `render()` looked innocent — the queries fire in the row machinery before the column code runs.

### Reproduction

```python
def size_choices():  # e.g. loaded from a reference table
    return {size.code: size.label for size in Size.objects.all()}

class Garment(models.Model):
    size = models.CharField(max_length=1, choices=size_choices)

class GarmentTable(tables.Table):
    size = tables.Column()  # accessor resolves to a choices field

# rendering N rows executes size_choices() — and its query — N times
```

### Suggested fix

When the model uses Django's *generated* display method (a `partialmethod` of `Model._get_FIELD_display`), resolve the label through a per-`BoundColumn` cache of `field.flatchoices`, evaluating the choices once per column per table render. A custom `get_FOO_display()` defined on the model would still be called per cell, since it may depend on instance state.

This is a sibling of #1029 — the same class of bug (hidden per-cell work in the cell-rendering path). I have a patch ready covering both and will open a PR shortly.

### Environment

- django-tables2 master (`e52d5bc`) / 3.0.0
- Django 6.0.3, Python 3.13, PostgreSQL
items.title: BoundRow calls get_FOO_display() for every cell; with callable choices (Django 5+) this can run a database query per cell

First, thanks for this wonderful library!

Second, today I learned that Excel doesn't assume CSV files are UTF-8 encoded unless a byte-order mark (BOM) is present.

Once upon a time, this was handled in tablib (https://github.com/jazzband/tablib/issues/18), but it appears that the architecture of tablib has changed since then and it's now returning streams that the user of that stream encodes.

After hacking at `django_tables2.export.export.TableExport`, it looks like a change to that class' response method would suffice:

```
    response.write(self.export().encode("utf-8-sig"))  # encode text stream with BOM
```

However, this is going to mess with other formats which return bytes.

Would you be open to a PR which tried to add BOMs to CSVs?
items.title: Add byte-order mark to CSV exports so that Excel knows they're UTF-8 encoded?

items.body:
After upgrading from 2.7.5 to 3.0.0, any page using {% render_table %} raises:

django.template.exceptions.TemplateSyntaxError: Could not parse the remainder:
'=column.order_by_alias.next' from 'table.prefixed_order_by_field=column.order_by_alias.next'
Root cause:

In 3.0.0 the {% querystring %} tag was rewritten as a @simple_tag. Django's standard parse_bits() parser (used by @simple_tag) requires keyword argument names to be plain identifiers — dots are not allowed.

However, the bundled django_tables2/table.html template still uses the old syntax:

{% querystring table.prefixed_order_by_field=column.order_by_alias.next %}
table.prefixed_order_by_field contains a dot, so parse_bits() rejects it at template compile time. The package's own template is incompatible with the package's own tag in this release.

Steps to reproduce:

Install django-tables2==3.0.0
Use {% render_table table %} with the default django_tables2/table.html template
Any request to that page raises TemplateSyntaxError
Expected behaviour: The bundled templates work with the bundled template tags.
Workaround: Pin to django-tables2==2.7.5
items.title: TemplateSyntaxError in table.html after upgrading to 3.0.0 — querystring tag breaks with dotted variable keys

We're using a "UserColumn" in which we're showing the user who owns a particular object in a table. However, we also want to use this same UserColumn when we're listing all our users. The way we figured out to accomplish this, is by using the `accessor` kwarg. 

I.e., when listing all UserLog; `UserColumn(accessor="user")`, when listing all User; `UserColumn(accessor=None)`.

The problem is that when inspecting `UserColumn.render(self, record)` the `accessor` is never `None`, even though we set it explicitly. We did some digging and found that in BoundColumn you have [these lines of code](https://github.com/jieter/django-tables2/blob/e52d5bc1b770f36935774261c3fb475a6e63ac4e/django_tables2/columns/base.py#L449):
```python
        if not column.accessor:
            column.accessor = Accessor(self.name)
        self.accessor = column.accessor
```
Thus, if our column definition is `name = UserColumn(accessor=None)` then `self.accessor` defaults to `name` rather than `None`.

a) Why does this exists/the rationale?, and 
b) should we use another kwarg to accomplish what we're trying to do?

TYIA.
items.title: Impossible to set `self.accessor` to `None`

items.body:
We're extending Nautobot (https://github.com/nautobot/nautobot) with a custom plugin, but receive an error originating from a `{% render_table table %}` call in a template in our plugin, resulting in the pages within nautobot to not be rendered. This error appeared when upgrading nautobot from version 2 to 3, but we traced the issue to this underlying django_tables2 package.

I haven't looked into the codebase, but threw claude at the task fwiw.
Below is a description and reproduction of the bug (written by Claude), which when fixed, should enable the use of `{% render_table %}` in nautobot plugins.

### Claude generated description and reproduction of the bug:
`RenderTableNode.render()` attaches the context to the table and removes it with `del table.context` in a `finally` block. This assumes only one `{% render_table %}` is ever active per instance. When the same instance is rendered re-entrantly (a custom table template containing `{% render_table %}`, a `before_render()` hook, or `TemplateColumn` rendering the same table), the inner call deletes `table.context` first and the outer `finally` raises:

```
AttributeError: 'MyTable' object has no attribute 'context'
```

https://github.com/jieter/django-tables2/blob/master/django_tables2/templatetags/django_tables2.py#L170

```python
class MyTable(tables.Table):
    name = tables.Column()

    def before_render(self, request):
        if not getattr(self, "rendering", False):
            self.rendering = True
            try:
                Template("{% load django_tables2 %}{% render_table table %}").render(
                    Context({"request": request, "table": self})
                )
            finally:
                self.rendering = False

table = MyTable([{"name": "Brad"}])
Template("{% load django_tables2 %}{% render_table table %}").render(
    Context({"request": request, "table": table})
)
# AttributeError: 'MyTable' object has no attribute 'context'
```

Saving and restoring the previous value instead of unconditionally deleting it fixes this.
items.title: render_table raises AttributeError when rendering the same table instance twice in one pass

items.body:
### Description

`TemplateColumn` with `template_name` causes an N+1 query problem on paginated tables. Each cell render triggers a `COUNT(*)` query against the table's queryset, because `context.flatten()` eagerly resolves lazy properties — including `table.paginator`, which calls `queryset.count()`.

A table with 50 rows and 2 `template_name` columns produces ~100 extra COUNT queries. A table with 100 rows and 4 such columns produces ~400. This scales linearly with rows * template_name columns.

`template_code` columns are **not** affected because they render with the `Context` object directly, which preserves lazy evaluation.

### Root Cause

In `templatecolumn.py`, the `render()` method takes two different paths:

```python
# Line 66-68: template_code path — renders with Context directly (lazy-safe)
if self.template_code:
    context["request"] = request
    return Template(self.template_code).render(context)

# Line 70: template_name path — flatten() eagerly resolves everything
else:
    return get_template(self.template_name).render(context.flatten(), request=request)
```

`context.flatten()` converts the `Context` stack into a plain `dict`, which eagerly accesses every property on objects in the context — including `table.paginator`. Django's `Paginator.__init__` calls `self.count` which executes `queryset.count()`.

### Reproduction

```python
import django_tables2 as tables

class MyTable(tables.Table):
    # This column triggers COUNT(*) per cell:
    name = tables.TemplateColumn(template_name="my_template.html")

    # This column does NOT:
    name2 = tables.TemplateColumn(template_code="{{ record.name }}")

    class Meta:
        model = MyModel
```

With Django Debug Toolbar or `CaptureQueriesContext`, you'll see one `SELECT COUNT(*) ...` query per cell for every `template_name` column, but zero extra queries for `template_code` columns.

### Suggested Fix

Use `template.template.render(context)` instead of `get_template(name).render(context.flatten())` to pass the `Context` object directly to the underlying `Template`, matching the `template_code` path:

```python
def render(self, record, table, value, bound_column, **kwargs):
    context = getattr(table, "context", Context())
    additional_context = {
        "default": bound_column.default,
        "column": bound_column,
        "record": record,
        "value": value,
        "row_counter": kwargs["bound_row"].row_counter,
    }
    additional_context.update(self.extra_context)
    with context.update(additional_context):
        request = getattr(table, "request", None)
        if self.template_code:
            context["request"] = request
            return Template(self.template_code).render(context)
        else:
            context["request"] = request
            template = get_template(self.template_name)
            return template.template.render(context)
```

This accesses `get_template().template` to get the underlying `Template` object, which accepts a `Context` directly — same as the `template_code` path. No `flatten()`, no eager property resolution, no spurious COUNT queries.

### Environment

- django-tables2 2.7.5 (also affects earlier versions — the code has been this way since at least 2.x)
- Django 6.0.3
- Python 3.12
- PostgreSQL (the COUNT queries are visible in any database backend)

### Impact

This is a silent performance regression that affects any paginated table using `template_name` columns. It's particularly severe on tables with many rows or multiple `template_name` columns. In our case, a 50-row table with 2 `template_name` columns went from 3 queries to 206.
items.title: TemplateColumn with template_name triggers COUNT(*) query per cell via context.flatten()

Where:
```python    
def get_context_data(self, **kwargs: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
    context = super().get_context_data(**kwargs)
    tables = self.get_tables()

    # apply prefixes and execute requestConfig for each table
    table_counter = count()
    for table in tables:
        table.prefix = table.prefix or self.table_prefix.format(next(table_counter))

        RequestConfig(self.request, paginate=self.get_table_pagination(table)).configure(table)

        context[self.get_context_table_name(table)] = list(tables)

    return context
```

Issue: 
`context[self.get_context_table_name(table)] = list(tables)`
List of all tables are put into context dict for each table context key inside table loop. This creates duplicate context data.

Resolved by:
`context[self.get_context_table_name(table)] = table`
Only put the table of current loop.
